Macworld

Apple’s new iPhone Duo is both big and small, and it’s more susceptible to knocks and drops than a standard iPhone with its folding function maybe taking a while to get used to. It’s the first iPhone that needs a case built around moving parts—namely the hinge. A case for a foldable can be made from one or two shells, with the additional question of covering the hinge or leaving it bare. The phone goes on sale October 23, and cases are already arriving.

iPhone Duo test criteria

We look for eight key criteria when testing each case.

Simon Jary

Protection: We checked corner reinforcement, camera and screen-edge protection, hinge coverage, and how much of the handset each shell covers. We did not run our own drop tests, so protection assessments are based on construction and coverage, and we note manufacturer claims as claims. Some case makers specify the exact measurements of their raised screen and camera edges, other do not.

Materials and grip: We assess surface texture, grip, finish, and visible fingerprint marks during handling. Common case materials include TPU (thermoplastic polyurethane, a flexible, durable plastic) and aramid fiber (a lightweight, high-strength synthetic fiber, best known through the Kevlar brand). The material alone does not establish how well a case protects the phone; construction and coverage also matter. Long-term wear, discoloration, and adhesive durability cannot be established during these initial checks.

Hinge protection and operation: Cases take different approaches to the Duo’s hinge: some include a protective cover, while others leave it exposed. We opened and closed each case on the dummy handset, checking for stiffness, rattling, gaps, and smooth movement of any hinge cover. We also checked whether both shells stayed firmly attached during opening and closing. These checks provide an initial assessment of the case’s construction and movement. We will assess the effect on the actual phone’s hinge movement or opening angle will require further testing with a working iPhone Duo.

Fit and installation: We used the dummy iPhone Duo to assess how securely each section fits the handset, the alignment of cutouts, and the ease of installation. We also checked the positioning and accessibility of button covers and port openings. Final fit and tolerances, button response, Touch ID operation, and cable fit will need confirmation with a retail iPhone Duo.

Slimness: The Duo’s thin profile is part of its appeal but this must be weighed against the backplate’s coverage and reinforcement. We penalize cases that add bulk without a clear benefit, but not where the protective benefits are worthwhile.

Extra functions: Some iPhone Duo cases include a kickstand for easier viewing. We assessed adjustability and how much bulk the stand adds. ESR’s Flex Stand, for example, rotates 180° and forms a protective guard around the camera bar when not in use. Other stands, such as those on the Torras Ostand and UAG Mouve XTE, rotate 360° and fold flat against the case backplate. The Moft Dynamic Folio uses an origami-like folding stand. Stability with a working iPhone Duo, both folded and unfolded, will require further testing because its weight and balance may differ from those of the dummy handset.

Colors and style: We assessed the range of colors and the quality of the finishes provided. Most of the color and pattern will be seen on the case’s backplate, but it should also be noticed on the front frame and hinge protector where present.

Magnetic accessory compatibility: We checked how securely magnetic chargers, power banks, wallets, and other accessories attached, and whether the case’s camera surround, hinge protection, or kickstand obstructed their fit. Because we used a dummy handset for our initial testing, these checks assess attachment and clearance only. We will test charging performance—including speed, heat, and reliability—once we have a working iPhone Duo.

There are two Apple-branded cases for the iPhone Duo. The basic version is called simply the Apple iPhone Duo Case. If you want everything to have an Apple logo on it, this is a solid choice you can’t go wrong with.

It’s a two-part design, with each side having its own thin cover and a protective frame around the edges. This leaves the phone’s hinge area “unobstructed” (which the pessimistic among us could also describe as “exposed”) so the device can fold and close completely flat without interference. Like most two-part cases without a hinge cover, it requires adhesive strips to ensure a secure fit, and so is not as easy to remove and reattach as magnetic cases such as Apple’s own Duo Folio case.

Made from polycarbonate with a matte coating, the case is available in two colors—Navy Blue and Sand—that match the Duo’s own Night Sky and Star White colors.

While it does protect the exterior display and the hinge, unlike the basic Apple Duo Case it doesn’t feature a protective frame for the phone’s edges. Somewhat remarkably, the MagSafe connection remains even when the stand cover is closed and will also work when it’s open. The Duo can wirelessly charge at up to 25W.

Again, the Navy Blue and Taupe case colors are suited to each of the two Duo appearances. It’s made with Apple’s leather-alternative TechWoven fabric, found on its standard iPhone cases. Unlike the basic Apple iPhone Duo Case, the Folio has a fabric hinge cover so that’s better protected. Benks makes some of our favorite standard iPhone cases, and its ArmorGrid Air Grand Combo for iPhone Duo matches the ArmorGrid case for iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. It’s a protection set that combines a front frame shielding the display perimeter and 1.3mm-thin back case made from super-tough Kevlar, and a screen protector for the front (not unfolded middle) screen. The whole package weighs a slight 23.5g in Beyond Blue (shown here); strangely the Obsidian Black version weighs less at just 18.8g and is marginally thinner at 1.2mm vs 1.3mm. You won’t notice the difference.

There’s no hinge protection, which keeps the Duo’s folding mechanism unencumbered and reduces the possible points of failure but also leaves this area of the Duo bare. Benks includes replacement adhesive strips in case you frequently remove the front frame.

The Kevlar back case features a diamond-pattern weave to create a structured, geometric texture that adds a little extra grip but nothing you really notice in hand. FAQ

Does the iPhone Duo need a case?

No phone needs a protective case until you drop or knock it. A case isn’t essential for the iPhone Duo, but it’s a sensible investment for a $1,999 foldable. Apple’s Ceramic Shield glass helps protect the displays, but the titanium edges and hinge remain vulnerable to accidental drops, scratches and dents. Unlike conventional iPhone cases, Duo designs must accommodate two halves and a slim cover-screen frame, often using adhesive to stay securely attached.

What to consider when choosing an iPhone Duo case?

Prioritize a precise fit, shock-absorbing corners and the level of coverage you think you need. Raised lips help protect the exterior display and camera, while a dedicated hinge guard covers the folding spine. Check that the case allows easy access to Touch ID and Camera Control without obstructing the inner display or folding mechanism. Since the Duo already weighs 8.9oz (254g), consider whether extra bulk from a kickstand or hinge protector is worthwhile. Choose a slim two-piece case for everyday protection or a hinge-cover design for additional coverage.

Will a case interfere with the iPhone Duo’s hinge or folding action?

A properly fitted iPhone Duo case shouldn’t interfere with folding, but poorly designed hinge covers can add bulk or restrict movement. Some two-piece cases leave the hinge exposed; others include a separate hinge cover, while dedicated covers provide an additional barrier against knocks and grit. However, hinge coverage doesn’t necessarily mean dust protection. Debris can collect between the case and phone, so remove the case periodically and gently clean both surfaces according to Apple’s care guidance. For cases secured with adhesive strips, follow the manufacturer’s removal and cleaning instructions, and check whether replacement strips are required before refitting.

Can I remove and reuse an iPhone Duo case?

That depends on how the case attaches. Some iPhone Duo cases use adhesive strips to secure the front frame or other components. Don’t assume those strips will retain their grip after removal: check whether the manufacturer allows reuse, supplies spare strips, or sells replacements.

A removable component isn’t necessarily reusable with the same adhesive. Before taking off an adhesive-mounted case for cleaning or swapping cases, follow its removal instructions and check what you’ll need to refit it securely.

Is a kickstand case necessary for the iPhone Duo?

If you regularly watch videos, make FaceTime calls or use your iPhone Duo for work, a kickstand case is a useful upgrade. It props up the larger inner display for hands-free viewing, video calls, recipes, and reading. Paired with a Bluetooth keyboard, it can also support light productivity. Some stands double as finger grips for safer handling. The main drawback is added thickness and weight, so look for a stable, well-integrated design that folds flat to the backplate or doubles as a camera bar.

Will MagSafe chargers, wallets, and power banks fit with these cases?

MagSafe uses magnets to align and attach compatible wireless chargers, power banks, wallets, and other accessories. The cases listed here are described as MagSafe compatible, but that doesn’t guarantee every accessory will fit.

Because the iPhone Duo is shorter than a conventional iPhone, larger magnetic wireless power banks and wallets may extend beyond its edges or overlap the camera bar. A case’s kickstand or hinge cover may also prevent an accessory from sitting flat or interfere with unfolding the phone.

Before buying, check the accessory’s dimensions and the case maker’s compatibility guidance. With the accessory attached, make sure it clears the cameras and allows the Duo to open fully. Some wallets and power banks may need to be removed before unfolding.

Our initial case assessments used a dummy handset, allowing us to assess physical clearance and attachment, but not wireless charging performance. We’ll add charging results and recommendations for specific accessories after testing them on a working iPhone Duo.

Would I do better getting AppleCare+ instead of a case?

A combination of slim case and AppleCare+ can offer a good balance between preserving the Duo’s design and protecting against costly accidents. A case helps prevent everyday scratches and knocks, while AppleCare+ covers eligible damage under the plan’s terms, subject to service fees. Theft and loss protection may also be available with a suitable plan. Check Apple’s current pricing and conditions before buying. For maximum peace of mind, use both: prevention for everyday mishaps and coverage for expensive repairs.

Apple’s new iPhone Duo is both big and small, and it’s more susceptible to knocks and drops than a standard iPhone with its folding function maybe taking a while to get used to. It’s the first iPhone that needs a case built around moving parts—namely the hinge. A case for a foldable can be made from one or two shells, with the additional question of covering the hinge or leaving it bare. The phone goes on sale October 23, and cases are already arriving.

iPhone Duo test criteria

We look for eight key criteria when testing each case.

Simon Jary

Protection: We checked corner reinforcement, camera and screen-edge protection, hinge coverage, and how much of the handset each shell covers. We did not run our own drop tests, so protection assessments are based on construction and coverage, and we note manufacturer claims as claims. Some case makers specify the exact measurements of their raised screen and camera edges, other do not.

Materials and grip: We assess surface texture, grip, finish, and visible fingerprint marks during handling. Common case materials include TPU (thermoplastic polyurethane, a flexible, durable plastic) and aramid fiber (a lightweight, high-strength synthetic fiber, best known through the Kevlar brand). The material alone does not establish how well a case protects the phone; construction and coverage also matter. Long-term wear, discoloration, and adhesive durability cannot be established during these initial checks.

Hinge protection and operation: Cases take different approaches to the Duo’s hinge: some include a protective cover, while others leave it exposed. We opened and closed each case on the dummy handset, checking for stiffness, rattling, gaps, and smooth movement of any hinge cover. We also checked whether both shells stayed firmly attached during opening and closing. These checks provide an initial assessment of the case’s construction and movement. We will assess the effect on the actual phone’s hinge movement or opening angle will require further testing with a working iPhone Duo.

Fit and installation: We used the dummy iPhone Duo to assess how securely each section fits the handset, the alignment of cutouts, and the ease of installation. We also checked the positioning and accessibility of button covers and port openings. Final fit and tolerances, button response, Touch ID operation, and cable fit will need confirmation with a retail iPhone Duo.

Slimness: The Duo’s thin profile is part of its appeal but this must be weighed against the backplate’s coverage and reinforcement. We penalize cases that add bulk without a clear benefit, but not where the protective benefits are worthwhile.

Extra functions: Some iPhone Duo cases include a kickstand for easier viewing. We assessed adjustability and how much bulk the stand adds. ESR’s Flex Stand, for example, rotates 180° and forms a protective guard around the camera bar when not in use. Other stands, such as those on the Torras Ostand and UAG Mouve XTE, rotate 360° and fold flat against the case backplate. The Moft Dynamic Folio uses an origami-like folding stand. Stability with a working iPhone Duo, both folded and unfolded, will require further testing because its weight and balance may differ from those of the dummy handset.

Colors and style: We assessed the range of colors and the quality of the finishes provided. Most of the color and pattern will be seen on the case’s backplate, but it should also be noticed on the front frame and hinge protector where present.

Magnetic accessory compatibility: We checked how securely magnetic chargers, power banks, wallets, and other accessories attached, and whether the case’s camera surround, hinge protection, or kickstand obstructed their fit. Because we used a dummy handset for our initial testing, these checks assess attachment and clearance only. We will test charging performance—including speed, heat, and reliability—once we have a working iPhone Duo.

FAQ

Does the iPhone Duo need a case?

No phone needs a protective case until you drop or knock it. A case isn’t essential for the iPhone Duo, but it’s a sensible investment for a $1,999 foldable. Apple’s Ceramic Shield glass helps protect the displays, but the titanium edges and hinge remain vulnerable to accidental drops, scratches and dents. Unlike conventional iPhone cases, Duo designs must accommodate two halves and a slim cover-screen frame, often using adhesive to stay securely attached.

What to consider when choosing an iPhone Duo case?

Prioritize a precise fit, shock-absorbing corners and the level of coverage you think you need. Raised lips help protect the exterior display and camera, while a dedicated hinge guard covers the folding spine. Check that the case allows easy access to Touch ID and Camera Control without obstructing the inner display or folding mechanism. Since the Duo already weighs 8.9oz (254g), consider whether extra bulk from a kickstand or hinge protector is worthwhile. Choose a slim two-piece case for everyday protection or a hinge-cover design for additional coverage.

Will a case interfere with the iPhone Duo’s hinge or folding action?

A properly fitted iPhone Duo case shouldn’t interfere with folding, but poorly designed hinge covers can add bulk or restrict movement. Some two-piece cases leave the hinge exposed; others include a separate hinge cover, while dedicated covers provide an additional barrier against knocks and grit. However, hinge coverage doesn’t necessarily mean dust protection. Debris can collect between the case and phone, so remove the case periodically and gently clean both surfaces according to Apple’s care guidance. For cases secured with adhesive strips, follow the manufacturer’s removal and cleaning instructions, and check whether replacement strips are required before refitting.

Can I remove and reuse an iPhone Duo case?

That depends on how the case attaches. Some iPhone Duo cases use adhesive strips to secure the front frame or other components. Don’t assume those strips will retain their grip after removal: check whether the manufacturer allows reuse, supplies spare strips, or sells replacements.

A removable component isn’t necessarily reusable with the same adhesive. Before taking off an adhesive-mounted case for cleaning or swapping cases, follow its removal instructions and check what you’ll need to refit it securely.

Is a kickstand case necessary for the iPhone Duo?

If you regularly watch videos, make FaceTime calls or use your iPhone Duo for work, a kickstand case is a useful upgrade. It props up the larger inner display for hands-free viewing, video calls, recipes, and reading. Paired with a Bluetooth keyboard, it can also support light productivity. Some stands double as finger grips for safer handling. The main drawback is added thickness and weight, so look for a stable, well-integrated design that folds flat to the backplate or doubles as a camera bar.

Will MagSafe chargers, wallets, and power banks fit with these cases?

MagSafe uses magnets to align and attach compatible wireless chargers, power banks, wallets, and other accessories. The cases listed here are described as MagSafe compatible, but that doesn’t guarantee every accessory will fit.

Because the iPhone Duo is shorter than a conventional iPhone, larger magnetic wireless power banks and wallets may extend beyond its edges or overlap the camera bar. A case’s kickstand or hinge cover may also prevent an accessory from sitting flat or interfere with unfolding the phone.

Before buying, check the accessory’s dimensions and the case maker’s compatibility guidance. With the accessory attached, make sure it clears the cameras and allows the Duo to open fully. Some wallets and power banks may need to be removed before unfolding.

Our initial case assessments used a dummy handset, allowing us to assess physical clearance and attachment, but not wireless charging performance. We’ll add charging results and recommendations for specific accessories after testing them on a working iPhone Duo.

Would I do better getting AppleCare+ instead of a case?

A combination of slim case and AppleCare+ can offer a good balance between preserving the Duo’s design and protecting against costly accidents. A case helps prevent everyday scratches and knocks, while AppleCare+ covers eligible damage under the plan’s terms, subject to service fees. Theft and loss protection may also be available with a suitable plan. Check Apple’s current pricing and conditions before buying. For maximum peace of mind, use both: prevention for everyday mishaps and coverage for expensive repairs.

The iPhone 15 and later have a USB-C port that can do more than charge your phone. You can plug in an external SSD, import photos from an SD card, connect wired headphones, or top up your AirPods or Apple Watch. Most USB-C iPhones can also connect to a monitor or TV. Here’s what works with your iPhone and which cables or adapters you’ll need.

Which iPhones have USB-C?

Apple switched from Lightning to USB-C with the iPhone 15 lineup in 2023. Every iPhone released since then has USB-C, but file transfer speeds and support for wired monitors and TVs vary by model.

The USB-C cable that comes with your iPhone supports charging and data transfers at up to 480Mbps. To get up to 10Gbps when copying files to an external SSD or computer, you’ll need a compatible iPhone from the first row, a USB-C cable rated for 10Gbps, and a drive or computer port that supports that speed.

1. Charge AirPods or an Apple Watch from your iPhone

Rival companies like Samsung have long supported reverse wireless charging, letting you turn your smartphone into a portable Qi charging pad. That usually means flipping your phone over and leaving it face down while the other device charges. With the iPhone 15, Apple introduced its own take on reverse charging using the USB-C port.

Your iPhone can deliver up to 4.5W of power, enough to top up your AirPods, Apple Watch, or even a friend’s compatible Android phone when you’re away from an outlet. For AirPods, grab a USB-C-to-USB-C or USB-C-to-Lightning cable, depending on the port on your charging case. To charge an Apple Watch, plug its USB-C magnetic charging cable into your iPhone and place the watch on the puck.

2. Connect an external SSD or USB flash drive

Most of us have seen the iPhone’s storage-full alert. If you’d rather keep a local copy of your files than rely on iCloud, you can plug an external SSD or USB flash drive into your iPhone’s USB-C port. It’s an easy way to move large files off your phone and free up space.

  1. Connect the drive.
  2. Open the Files app.
  3. Tap Browse.
  4. Select the drive under Locations.
  5. Now you can open files on the drive or copy them to and from your iPhone.

A compact Samsung Type-C Flash Drive ($80) is a handy option for everyday transfers. If you’re using a drive that needs more power than the iPhone can supply, connect it through a powered USB hub.

If you shoot ProRes video on an iPhone 15 Pro through iPhone 18 Pro, including the Pro Max models, you can record directly to a compatible external SSD. ProRes files take up a lot of space, so recording to a drive can help you shoot longer without filling up your iPhone. For 4K at 60 fps, use an exFAT-formatted SSD that can sustain write speeds of at least 220 MB/s and a 10Gbps USB-C data cable.

Foundry

3. Import photos and videos from an SD card

Photographers and videographers love the handy SD card slots on the MacBook Pro and Mac Studio, and a wired SD card reader brings that same convenience to your iPhone. While many newer cameras support wireless photo transfers through their companion apps, plugging in the card can be quicker when you have a lot of photos or videos to import.

Plug a reader such as Apple’s USB-C to SD Card Reader ($39) into your iPhone’s charging port and insert the card from your camera. Open Photos, tap Import, then choose Import All or select the photos and videos you want to copy. To browse the card’s folders or copy other files, open Files, tap Browse, and select the card under Locations.

You can also use the same reader with a USB-C Mac or iPad when you want to edit on a larger screen. See our roundup of the best USB-C adapters.

4. Connect your iPhone to a monitor or TV

If you’re staying at a hotel that blocks wireless casting, you may still be able to mirror your iPhone’s screen by plugging it into the TV. First, check your model. If your iPhone supports wired video and the TV has an accessible HDMI port, use a USB-C-to-HDMI cable or plug Apple’s USB-C Digital AV Multiport Adapter ($69) into your iPhone and connect it to the TV with a separate HDMI cable. If your monitor has a USB-C video input, you can plug your iPhone directly into it using the cable that came with the monitor or another USB-C cable that supports DisplayPort video. Unfortunately, the charging cable included with your iPhone won’t work for this.

Apple introduced wireless CarPlay a few years ago, but if your car only supports wired CarPlay, you’ll still need to plug your iPhone into the car’s USB port. Make sure the cable supports both data and charging, is long enough to reach the port, and is flexible enough to route around any knobs or vents.

It’s been a loaded fall for Apple fans. Over the past couple of months, the company launched around a dozen new products, including several brand-new products rumored for years. Many have been sold out for weeks and months, and millions of people are still basking in the new-device glow of the iPhone Duo, PROLED MacBook Pro, and HomeView.

Even so, there are enough issues with the new devices, not to mention high prices, to convince many users to stick with their existing setups for another year. Apple hasn’t forgotten you. In just a few weeks, iOS 27.3 and the rest of the OS updates will bring a fresh wave of useful additions to older devices. So even if you’re skipping the hardware upgrades this season, your iPhone, iPad, and Mac are getting a bunch of excellent new features before the year is up.

The good dark web

Seven years ago, Apple brought system-wide dark mode to the iPhone with iOS 13. While most popular apps have implemented support for the theme, many websites remain restricted to the light look, contributing to eye strain when browsing at night. Safari on iOS 27.3—as well as iPadOS and macOS—remedies the situation by implementing an Adaptive Dark Mode toggle.

When enabled, the feature automatically adapts bright webpages to dark mode by tweaking the colors of the background, text, and other assets. The perk is completely optional, and you can exclude individual websites if you so prefer. While this can effectively replace dedicated Safari extensions that serve the same purpose, third-party tools will remain relevant for some power users. After all, Apple’s implementation isn’t personalizable and doesn’t provide the same level of control. It just works.

Other Safari additions offered by iOS 27.3 beta include a vertical tab layout solely on the iPhone Duo. (If you haven’t bought a Duo, worry not, as iPadOS and macOS 27.3 beta bring the same feature to your existing devices.) This stacks open Safari tabs vertically along the side, as opposed to the traditional horizontal row.

And speaking of macOS, this beta release also ports the Now Playing Live Activity’s colorful waveform on the touchscreen MacBook Pro to all other Macs. While the Dynamic Island itself remains a high-end exclusive, older Macs won’t miss out on the experience anymore.

Mahmoud Itani/Foundry

Functional gains

For years, Apple Fitness+ has offered hundreds of guided workout videos and meditation sessions, helping subscribers stay active. With watchOS 27.3 beta, the paid service adds a new Gym Strength feature that can build a custom workout plan based on your available equipment, schedule, and readiness. Once the plan is set up, you simply follow the selected trainer’s instructions, and you get to adjust the load and rep counts if the defaults don’t match your level. To use Gym Strength, your iPhone or iPad must also be running the OS 27.3 beta—not just your Apple Watch.

Karaoke camera

Apple Music is another subscription service getting some love with iOS 27.3 beta. After updating your iPhone, a new Selfie Sing button will appear when viewing the lyrics of compatible songs. The feature upgrades the existing karaoke experience by letting you record a short video of yourself with an overlay of the track’s title, cover, and real-time lyrics. 

It’s a fun perk that makes sharing music with friends or on social media more engaging and personal, but the supported catalog appears to be very limited for now. To spare you from hunting, Apple has compiled some of the eligible songs in a dedicated playlist.

Mahmoud Itani/Foundry

Déjà Duo

With the iPhone Duo launch, Apple introduced a revamped StandBy mode that works exclusively on its foldable without needing a charger. The redesigned experience unlocks support for more advanced color and layout customizations, similar to those available with Apple Watch faces. Thankfully, iOS 27.3 beta brings some of these options to regular iPhones—although charging is still required. After installing the update, tap and hold on the screen in StandBy mode to add, edit, or delete a custom look.

Speaking of the iPhone Duo, the second beta of iOS 27.3 also introduces the ability to unlock the phone with the front camera when it’s closed as long as Touch ID has been used within 45 minutes.

Agentic age

iOS 27.3 beta boosts Siri AI’s agentic capabilities by letting it execute complex in-app tasks using voice or text commands. The upgraded functionality is already live in most of Apple’s built-in applications, including Mail, Messages, Calendar, Safari, Files, and Reminders. Managing Safari tabs, organizing files, and scheduling iMessages are some of the handy actions you can try right away. If you’re not sure where to start, you can launch the desired app and ask Siri what it can do.

With this OS release, Apple also enables third-party developers to adopt similar advancements in their apps using the App Intents framework. And with the new Siri AI skills, developers can teach the assistant to merge multiple actions into one. This should simplify controlling apps in a hands-free manner.

Mahmoud Itani/Foundry

Healthy facelift

Lastly, iOS 27.3 beta brings back the overhauled Health app that Apple briefly tested during the iOS 27.2 beta cycle. The new interface surfaces relevant health and fitness data in a more visually appealing way and introduces all-new insights like Health Age and AI-powered tips.

iOS 27.3 is currently available to developers and public beta testers. If you are familiar with the associated risks—which include the potential of bricking your device and losing local data—and would like to try the new features today, you can enroll in either beta program and download the available prerelease builds on any of your compatible Apple devices. But it won’t be long before all of these updates arrive for everyone; we’re expecting the final versions to launch around mid-December.

FAQ

1.

How much time does Apple Watch take to fast charge?

The Apple Watch battery life is notoriously short between charges so fast charging is a great way to keep your smart timepiece topped up and ready for action.

Using a Fast Charger cable, you’ll get fully powered up in the shortest time so look for Watch chargers that support fast-charging.

  • Apple Watch Series 7, Series 8, and Series 9: Charge from 0% to 80% in about 45 minutes.
  • Apple Watch Series 10 and later: Charge from 0% to 80% in about 30 minutes.
  • Apple Watch Ultra and Ultra 2: Charge from 0% to 80% in about an hour.
  • Apple Watch Ultra 4: Charge from 0% to 80% in about 45 minutes.
  • Apple Watch Ultra 3: Charge from 0% to 80% in about 45 minutes.
  • Apple Watch SE 3: Charges from 0% to 80% in about 45 minutes.

An eight-minute charge should power your Watch for eight hours of sleep tracking.

Fast charging requires at least a 20W USB-C charger.

See How to fast charge Apple Watch for more information.

2.

Which Apple Watch models can fast charge?

The following Apple Watch models support Fast Charge: Apple Watch Series 7 and later, Apple Watch Ultra and later.

The original Apple Watch SE does not support Fast Charge, but the Apple Watch SE 3 does.

3.

How can I see my Apple Watch battery percentage?

To see how much power remains on your Apple Watch, hold the bottom of the screen and swipe up to open the Control Center. You can add the battery life percentage to the watch face by adding a battery complication, in this way:

  1. Hold the display, then tap Edit
  2. Swipe left to the end to see if the watch face includes a possible battery complication
  3. Tap the complication to select it, then turn the Digital Crown to choose the battery complication
  4. To save your changes, press the Digital Crown, then tap the face to switch to it.

You can also add a battery widget to show the battery percentage of a connected Apple Watch on your iPhone.

4.

How to save battery power on the Apple watch

When you can’t get to your Apple Watch charger fast enough and the Watch battery is dangerously low, you can eke out the remaining battery charge by saving power.

The easiest way save battery life is to turn on Low Power Mode. This turns off Always On Display, background heart rate and blood oxygen measurements, plus heart rate notifications. Cellular access is also turned off in Low Power Mode. If you’re just going for a walk, then maybe you don’t need the heart monitor on—although this may impact your Exercise score, it could keep your Watch going till you get back to base and a charging socket.

To turn on Low Power Mode, tap the side button on your Apple Watch to open Control Center, and select the battery percentage. Then tap Low Power Mode.

Apple states that “other notifications may be delayed, emergency alerts may not arrive, and certain cellular and Wi-Fi connections are limited” in Low Power Mode.

When the Watch battery is charged to 80%, Low Power Mode turns off automatically.

Other Apple Watch battery saving tips include:

  1. Don’t use an Exercise or other tracking.
  2. If you are exercising you can still save some battery by turning on Low Power Mode—open the Watch app on your iPhone, and scroll to Workout where you can turn Low Power Mode on by tapping the slider on the right. To further conserve battery life, turn on Fewer GPS and Heart Rate Readings by tapping the slider.
  3. Turn off Always On Display in the Settings app
  4. Turn off the Wake Screen so that when you raise the watch to your face the screen doesn’t automatically turn on. Tap the screen or press the Digital Crown to manually wake up the screen instead. Open Settings on your Apple Watch. Select General > Display & Brightness. Turn off Wake on Wrist Raise by tapping the slider.
  5. Turn off background apps: push the side button (not the digital crown) and release it; then scroll through the running apps using the digital crown; close the apps by swiping from left to right and tapping on the “X”
  6. Turn off the heart rate monitor and advanced health tracking in the Watch app on your iPhone: Privacy
  7. Turn off voice assistant Siri—which is always listening for your commands—in Apple Watch Settings
  8. Turn on Theater mode, which prevents the Apple Watch display from turning on when you raise your wrist, and also turns on Silent Mode
  9. Turn on Silent Mode
  10. Use a darker watch face as black pixels use less power than bright ones such as Mickey Mouse or the Activity Face
  11. In extreme circumstances when you know you’ll need your Apple Watch later but not right now, turn off your Apple Watch by pressing and holding the side button until you see the Power Off slider
  12. Unpair AirPods from your Apple Watch in Settings.
  13. Always keep your Watch software up to date. Some Watch software updates are specifically to improve battery life, while others keep your Watch operating as efficiently as possible. In the Watch app on your iPhone, go to My Watch > General > Software Update.
  14. Optimized Battery Charging is turned on by default when you set up your Apple Watch, but check it’s on by opening Settings on the Apple Watch,a nd then selecting Battery > Battery Health. Turn Optimized Battery Charging on via the slider. See more on Optimized Battery Charging below.

See: How to improve Apple Watch battery life for more advice.

5.

How to turn on Low Power Mode on the Apple Watch

When its battery charge falls to 10% or lower, your Apple Watch alerts you and suggests that you enter Low Power Mode.

  1. Hold the bottom of the Watch screen, then swipe up to open Control Center.
  2. Tap the battery percentage icon, then turn on Low Power Mode.
  3. Scroll down, and tap Turn On Low Power Mode.
6.

Optimize Apple Watch Charging

The Apple Watch Optimized Battery Charging feature uses on-device machine learning to discover your charging habits over time along with your daily usage to either charge the Watch to an optimized level or charge it to full in order to improve the lifespan of your Watch battery.

This will slow down the wear on your Watch battery to improve its lifespan by reducing the time your Apple Watch spends fully charged. When turned on, your watch delays charging past 80% in certain situations, so that the battery level remains between 75-80%. Optimised Battery Charging is only activated when your watch predicts it will be connected to a charger for an extended period of time, and still aims to ensure your Apple Watch is fully charged when removed from the charger.

If, for example, you mostly leave your Watch on charge overnight, Optimised Battery Charging will slow down the charging to make it more efficient over the period you are usually asleep, while still making sure that the battery is full and ready for your daytime usage by the time you wake up.

FAQ

1.

How much time does Apple Watch take to fast charge?

The Apple Watch battery life is notoriously short between charges so fast charging is a great way to keep your smart timepiece topped up and ready for action.

Using a Fast Charger cable, you’ll get fully powered up in the shortest time so look for Watch chargers that support fast-charging.

  • Apple Watch Series 7, Series 8, and Series 9: Charge from 0% to 80% in about 45 minutes.
  • Apple Watch Series 10 and later: Charge from 0% to 80% in about 30 minutes.
  • Apple Watch Ultra and Ultra 2: Charge from 0% to 80% in about an hour.
  • Apple Watch Ultra 4: Charge from 0% to 80% in about 45 minutes.
  • Apple Watch Ultra 3: Charge from 0% to 80% in about 45 minutes.
  • Apple Watch SE 3: Charges from 0% to 80% in about 45 minutes.

An eight-minute charge should power your Watch for eight hours of sleep tracking.

Fast charging requires at least a 20W USB-C charger.

See How to fast charge Apple Watch for more information.

2.

Which Apple Watch models can fast charge?

The following Apple Watch models support Fast Charge: Apple Watch Series 7 and later, Apple Watch Ultra and later.

The original Apple Watch SE does not support Fast Charge, but the Apple Watch SE 3 does.

3.

How can I see my Apple Watch battery percentage?

To see how much power remains on your Apple Watch, hold the bottom of the screen and swipe up to open the Control Center. You can add the battery life percentage to the watch face by adding a battery complication, in this way:

  1. Hold the display, then tap Edit
  2. Swipe left to the end to see if the watch face includes a possible battery complication
  3. Tap the complication to select it, then turn the Digital Crown to choose the battery complication
  4. To save your changes, press the Digital Crown, then tap the face to switch to it.

You can also add a battery widget to show the battery percentage of a connected Apple Watch on your iPhone.

4.

How to save battery power on the Apple watch

When you can’t get to your Apple Watch charger fast enough and the Watch battery is dangerously low, you can eke out the remaining battery charge by saving power.

The easiest way save battery life is to turn on Low Power Mode. This turns off Always On Display, background heart rate and blood oxygen measurements, plus heart rate notifications. Cellular access is also turned off in Low Power Mode. If you’re just going for a walk, then maybe you don’t need the heart monitor on—although this may impact your Exercise score, it could keep your Watch going till you get back to base and a charging socket.

To turn on Low Power Mode, tap the side button on your Apple Watch to open Control Center, and select the battery percentage. Then tap Low Power Mode.

Apple states that “other notifications may be delayed, emergency alerts may not arrive, and certain cellular and Wi-Fi connections are limited” in Low Power Mode.

When the Watch battery is charged to 80%, Low Power Mode turns off automatically.

Other Apple Watch battery saving tips include:

  1. Don’t use an Exercise or other tracking.
  2. If you are exercising you can still save some battery by turning on Low Power Mode—open the Watch app on your iPhone, and scroll to Workout where you can turn Low Power Mode on by tapping the slider on the right. To further conserve battery life, turn on Fewer GPS and Heart Rate Readings by tapping the slider.
  3. Turn off Always On Display in the Settings app
  4. Turn off the Wake Screen so that when you raise the watch to your face the screen doesn’t automatically turn on. Tap the screen or press the Digital Crown to manually wake up the screen instead. Open Settings on your Apple Watch. Select General > Display & Brightness. Turn off Wake on Wrist Raise by tapping the slider.
  5. Turn off background apps: push the side button (not the digital crown) and release it; then scroll through the running apps using the digital crown; close the apps by swiping from left to right and tapping on the “X”
  6. Turn off the heart rate monitor and advanced health tracking in the Watch app on your iPhone: Privacy
  7. Turn off voice assistant Siri—which is always listening for your commands—in Apple Watch Settings
  8. Turn on Theater mode, which prevents the Apple Watch display from turning on when you raise your wrist, and also turns on Silent Mode
  9. Turn on Silent Mode
  10. Use a darker watch face as black pixels use less power than bright ones such as Mickey Mouse or the Activity Face
  11. In extreme circumstances when you know you’ll need your Apple Watch later but not right now, turn off your Apple Watch by pressing and holding the side button until you see the Power Off slider
  12. Unpair AirPods from your Apple Watch in Settings.
  13. Always keep your Watch software up to date. Some Watch software updates are specifically to improve battery life, while others keep your Watch operating as efficiently as possible. In the Watch app on your iPhone, go to My Watch > General > Software Update.
  14. Optimized Battery Charging is turned on by default when you set up your Apple Watch, but check it’s on by opening Settings on the Apple Watch,a nd then selecting Battery > Battery Health. Turn Optimized Battery Charging on via the slider. See more on Optimized Battery Charging below.

See: How to improve Apple Watch battery life for more advice.

5.

How to turn on Low Power Mode on the Apple Watch

When its battery charge falls to 10% or lower, your Apple Watch alerts you and suggests that you enter Low Power Mode.

  1. Hold the bottom of the Watch screen, then swipe up to open Control Center.
  2. Tap the battery percentage icon, then turn on Low Power Mode.
  3. Scroll down, and tap Turn On Low Power Mode.
6.

Optimize Apple Watch Charging

The Apple Watch Optimized Battery Charging feature uses on-device machine learning to discover your charging habits over time along with your daily usage to either charge the Watch to an optimized level or charge it to full in order to improve the lifespan of your Watch battery.

This will slow down the wear on your Watch battery to improve its lifespan by reducing the time your Apple Watch spends fully charged. When turned on, your watch delays charging past 80% in certain situations, so that the battery level remains between 75-80%. Optimised Battery Charging is only activated when your watch predicts it will be connected to a charger for an extended period of time, and still aims to ensure your Apple Watch is fully charged when removed from the charger.

If, for example, you mostly leave your Watch on charge overnight, Optimised Battery Charging will slow down the charging to make it more efficient over the period you are usually asleep, while still making sure that the battery is full and ready for your daytime usage by the time you wake up.

Should you buy an old pair of AirPods?

Older-generation AirPods can be a good buy at the right clearance price. Compare their actual selling price with the discounted price of their replacement, rather than focusing on the percentage saving from an old launch price. A substantial discount can make an older pair worthwhile; a small difference may leave you sacrificing useful features for little saving.

AirPods 4 are harder to recommend now that AirPods 5 include Active Noise Cancellation as standard, starting at the same $129 price previously charged for AirPods 4 without ANC. Check which AirPods 4 version you’re buying—there were models with and without noise cancellation—and look for a substantial saving over AirPods 5.

AirPods Pro 2 remain worth considering if they’re significantly cheaper than Pro 3. However, the newer model improves fit, noise cancellation, and battery life, while adding heart-rate sensing. Compare their sale prices carefully: a strong Pro 3 discount could make the older pair’s clearance offer less attractive.

The original AirPods Max also need a substantial discount to justify choosing them over Max 2. The newer headphones add the H2 chip, improved noise cancellation, and features including Adaptive Audio and Conversation Awareness. Check the generation rather than relying on the charging port alone: the original AirPods Max were also sold in a USB-C version.

Buying older stock new is different from buying used or refurbished AirPods. For those pairs, check the stated condition, charging case, warranty, and returns policy, and buy from a reputable seller. Be cautious about battery condition and unusually low marketplace prices, since convincing counterfeits can resemble genuine AirPods. Our guide explains how to spot fake AirPods.

For more advice, see our AirPods buying guide and guide to the best time to buy AirPods.

AirPods deals to avoid

Foundry

Check exactly what an offer includes before comparing prices. Different charging-case packages can affect features and value, so make sure you’re comparing equivalent versions. Also check any spending requirements, contracts, or rebates attached to offers advertising “free” AirPods.

Judge the price against previous selling prices as well as the advertised discount. A large saving from the recommended retail price doesn’t necessarily mean a particularly good deal if retailers regularly charge less.

Check whether the listing is for a new, refurbished, or used pair. For used or refurbished AirPods, look for clear information about condition, warranty, and returns coverage. Battery condition deserves particular caution: a low purchase price may be less attractive if listening time has deteriorated.

Finally, check who is selling and dispatching your order, particularly when shopping through a marketplace. Unusually low prices from unfamiliar sellers warrant caution, since counterfeit AirPods can look convincing. Our guide explains how to tell if AirPods are fake.

How we choose AirPods deals

Macworld’s editors have decades of experience with Apple devices, and our recommendations draw on hands-on AirPods reviews. We consider sound quality, noise cancellation, comfort, battery life, and everyday use – not just the specifications or advertised saving.

Our testing helps us explain which features are worth paying for. For example, our AirPods Pro 3 review assessed how securely the redesigned ear tips stayed in place during exercise, checked battery life against Apple’s claims, and evaluated the heart-rate sensor. Our AirPods Max 2 review weighed their excellent sound and noise cancellation against drawbacks including weight and the Smart Case.

We combine those findings with current prices and previous lows to judge whether an offer represents good value. Our Best AirPods guide explains why the most expensive model isn’t necessarily the best choice for everyone: fit, listening habits, and the features you need all matter.

Slow Horses, one of the most consistently popular and successful shows to emerge from Apple’s TV streaming venture, has been renewed for a ninth and tenth season. This contradicts seemingly definitive comments from one of the show’s stars a few days ago indicating that it would conclude with the eighth season.

Deadline broke the news that Slow Horses “[had] been greenlighted by Apple TV for unprecedented ninth and 10th seasons.” It wasn’t clear where the site originally obtained this information, but it claimed to have confirmation from Apple itself. And Macworld has since got in touch with the company, which told us: “Today [Tuesday, November 19], Apple TV announced seasons nine and ten for Emmy and BAFTA Award-winning, darkly comedic spy drama Slow Horses.” It’s official.

This is nevertheless surprising, because Olivia Cooke, a member of the main cast in the first season and a returning star in the most recent sixth, recently indicated (with the minor caveat of “never say never”) that it was drawing to a close. Speaking to The Times on November 14 while shooting the eighth season, Cooke went on record with the following surprisingly forthright remarks:

“I am shooting the last season!” she says. Is she supposed to say that? She laughs, then frowns. “Never say never!” she adds, backtracking. “But I think that’s what we’ve been told and it definitely feels like we are ending. We’re all melancholy, distracted. Yesterday, I got in the make-up chair and cried. The show’s been a shining light and I’ve told my partner I need two weeks to get over it. I’m going to be depressed.”

Aside from Cooke’s remarks, it seemed logical to expect a hiatus after the eighth season, at the very least, because the showrunners are running out of source material. The seventh and eighth seasons will be based on the Mick Herron novels Bad Actors and Clown Town, and he hasn’t written any more. Either he will need to get writing, or the show will need to go beyond his books.

Update: According to Apple, all services have been restored and are working normally.

The past week has been a nonstop parade of important network outages, from a big Microsoft fiasco to the FAA grounding planes and more, including network issues at the NSA and JPMorgan Chase & Co. Now, it looks like it’s Apple’s turn.

For the last couple of hours, several of Apple’s network services have been experiencing problems. The System Status page has shown various services in various states of operation, from iCloud Mail to Apple Music and News, though most of them have returned to “green” status. Several internal Apple networking services for employees are said to be affected as well.

At the time of this writing, there are scattered issues with some of the School Management services and AppleCare’s on-device signup, volume purchases, and the App Store. It is not clear how widespread these issues are, however, and two of our editors in the U.S. were able to use the App Store just fine, for example.

In a statement to Bloomberg, Apple said, “Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning. We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible.” Apple also said the problems do not stem from a cyberattack, echoing the sentiment from Microsoft and others. Apparently it’s just been a really bad week.

Macworld

In October, Apple announced that it was going to change how it implements Full Disk Access control in macOS. Users were going to have to perform “very explicit user action” to grant FDA to an app, which is a change from before, when apps could prompt users to flip switches on in System Settings to allow FDA.

The change is coming to macOS 27.3, and it was recently unveiled in the macOS 27.3 beta 2 that was released on Monday. Apple released a note to developers notifying them about the change, stating that the changes “empower [users] to make informed decisions about their own data and privacy.”

The new FDA UI was posted online by madeby_ldt, and it’s much more detailed and explicit. When an app asks for FDA, users will now be able to see what data the app wants to collect and grant permission to certain types of access. For example, the ChatGPT app wants access to be able to “Read, Change, Delete, and Export All Your Data,” “View Hidden and Recently Deleted Photos,” and “View History and Browse as You.” You’ll be able to allow or deny access to each of those requests.

The example provided uses ChatGPT, which is no coincidence. Chatbots and other AI apps want as much access to your data as they can get—it’s how they function and are able to tailor responses to your specific needs. AI apps aren’t the only ones that want FDA, but they grow more popular every day, and a lot of users are naive about how they work. Apple’s changes to FDA are one way to bring awareness of AI demands to the user.

Apple is expected to release macOS 27.3 in early December. Keep track of the latest with macOS 27 in our superguide.

https://nintendolife.com/features/talkin.html:
Nintendo's guide aims to highlight the benefits.

Over the summer, I replayed Ocarina of Time (1998) with my kids. I hadn't intended to, but it dawned on me that once the gorgeous remake landed, the original's visible polygons might not hold the same appeal for them. It was selfish, really, but I wanted them to experience the original magic as I did.

I held the pad but let them direct me, staying silent or feigning ignorance about puzzle solutions, letting them speculate and point out chests and switches I'd intentionally run past, involving them in an adventure they don't quite have the dexterity to control themselves.
